newsitem.title: UK: IGC raises 1996 wheat output but stocks, trade low.
newsitem.headline: IGC raises 1996 wheat output but stocks, trade low.

text.p: The International Grains Council (IGC) raised its forecast for the 1996 world wheat harvest on Thursday by 8.0 million tonnes from its previous estimate to 571 million tonnes.
In its latest monthly report, the IGC saw world 1996/97 wheat trade at 88 million tonnes, down one million tonnes from last month's figure and the lowest level since 1985/86.

Wheat stocks were forecast to rise to 104 million tonnes at the end of the 1996/97 crop year, 3.0 million tonnes higher than the previous estimate and the lowest since 1980 except for last year, the IGC said.
A "significant rebuilding" of stocks was expected, it added.

The modest increase in wheat stocks was entirely attributable to the five major wheat exporting countries whose carryovers were now expected to increase from a 20-year low of 28 million tonnes in 1996 to 38 million tonnes, the IGC said.
The sharp rise in wheat production was mainly due to higher expectations in the European Union (EU) and Australia.
The EU wheat output was forecast at 96.1 million tonnes, 3.1 million up on the previous forecast, with higher yields expected to give rise to better harvests in France and Britain.
France was expected to produce a bumper crop with its larger sowing area and higher yields. British winter wheat yields were said to be better than expected.
"There was a huge increase in yields that came rather late in the season," said Bill de Maria, the IGC's assistant executive director.
The IGC said Spain had made a big recovery from drought conditions and production was expected to double.
The IGC raised its forecast for Australian 1996 wheat production by 1.5 million tonnes to 19.0 million tonnes.
"The outlook is better because sowings are up," he said.
The IGC left its previous production forecasts for Russia and China unchanged, at 34.0 and 106.0 million tonnes respectively, but raised the U.S. estimate by 1.3 million tonnes to 62.5 million.
"The quality of the (U.S.) crop is reported as excellent with high test weight and low moisture content in spring wheats," the IGC said.
De Maria said the forecast for world wheat trade was lower because of a lower figure for China and Iraq, as the UN-sponsored oil-for-food deal had not been implemented.
Chinese wheat trade was seen at 8.0 million tonnes, down 1.0 million on the last estimate, and the Iraqi figure was pegged 800,000 tonnes lower at 1.2 million tonnes.
"Those decreases are offset by larger expectations of feed wheat imports into Korea," de Maria said.
